::: {.kw-overview}
This fortnight brings rare evidence of clinical decision support changing what happens to patients: a deterioration model wired to automatic rapid response calls across eleven US hospitals was associated with lower risk-adjusted mortality, and a German randomised trial found that AI-written lay summaries sent before clinic shortened consultations and improved how patients rated them. Two papers from South West London show the two faces of medical imaging AI in the NHS: chest X-ray triage cut the time to CT for suspected lung cancer, but the same commercial platform's external validation for nasogastric tube position missed 17 unsafe tubes in a year of silent running, which the authors say may make it unsuitable as the primary check. A randomised reader study on head CT adds that clinicians both over-trust wrong AI advice and ignore correct advice, and that the second error costs more. On ambient documentation and drafted patient messages, two large health-system studies find real but modest gains in documentation time and turnaround, without clear relief from after-hours work. A benchmark of six commercial large language models against Choosing Wisely scenarios rounds out the issue: false restraint was rare, but overuse clustered in a few familiar low-value tests, a safety point worth knowing before using these models for ordering decisions. Note: no full texts were available via PubMed Central for the selected papers in this run, so every summary below is grounded strictly in the PubMed abstract.
:::

---

### 1. [Implementation of an AI-Triggered Rapid Response - Association with Mortality.](https://doi.org/10.1056/AIoa2500973)
[Nahass TA, Hanna JS, Liu N, Martinez N, Halm EA, Rockman A, Roy J, Gilligan C, Murtha AP, Gracias V, Anderson RA, O'Mahony SP. *NEJM AI*, 2026. PMID: 42932707.]{.kw-ref}

This quasi-experimental study compared adult medical-surgical admissions before and after a regional US health system switched on the Epic Deterioration Index, a machine learning deterioration score, linked to electronic alerts and automatic push notifications to the rapid response team. Rollout was staggered across 11 hospitals of different types, and the analysis covered 23,132 patients whose score reached 60 or more between October 2022 and August 2024. After implementation, 46.6% of eligible encounters triggered a push notification, and rapid response activations rose from 25.3% to 37.5% (adjusted OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.61–1.88). Unadjusted in-hospital mortality fell from 23.1% to 18.6%, and after adjustment for age, comorbidity, hospital type, the score itself and clustering by hospital the odds of death were lower after implementation (adjusted OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.74–0.91). Escalations of care did not increase significantly (1.0% vs 1.1%). The comparator is the same hospitals in an earlier period, not a concurrent control, so secular trends and other quality work could explain part of the difference. For NHS trusts weighing deterioration models alongside NEWS2, the point is that any benefit seems to come from pairing the score with an automatic, staffed response rather than from the score alone, and a randomised or stepped-wedge evaluation would still be needed.

### 2. [Effect of Previsit AI-Generated Document Summaries on Consultation Time and Patient-Physician Communication - The AI-INFOCARE Randomized Controlled Trial.](https://doi.org/10.1056/AIoa2600136)
[Benker-Hasani E, Richter S, Buszello C, Willkommen S, Prem MG, Hijazi M, Martin KD, Juratli T, Eyüpoglu IY, Polanski WH. *NEJM AI*, 2026. PMID: 42932468.]{.kw-ref}

In a single-centre trial at a German neurosurgical outpatient clinic, 300 adults were randomised to usual care or usual care plus a quality-checked, AI-generated plain-language summary of their medical findings (Simply Onno), given before the consultation. The primary outcome was the patient's rating of the doctor-patient interaction on the FAPI questionnaire, which was modestly higher with the summary (4.42 vs 4.25; difference 0.17, 95% CI 0.05–0.29), mainly through better scores for shared decision-making. Patients also felt their autonomy was better supported, although the doctors rated their own autonomy support slightly lower in the intervention arm. Median consultations were 25 minutes with the summary and 33 without, a relative reduction of about 21% (ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.70–0.88). Perceived empathy did not differ, and a small rise in encounter difficulty was compatible with no change. Secondary outcomes were not corrected for multiple comparisons, and the trial did not measure clinical outcomes or the work of checking the summaries. For UK outpatient services under time pressure, this is the first randomised signal that pre-clinic AI explanations of letters and reports can help, but it needs replication beyond one specialty and one hospital.

### 3. [Early Clinical Evaluation of AI Triage of Chest Radiographs: Time to Diagnosis for Suspected Cancer and Number of Urgent CT Referrals.](https://doi.org/10.1056/AIcs2500539)
[Storey M, Packer J, Grandal NS, Rhodes A, Moon J, Togher D, Abubacker Z, Rickaby S, Dean G, Shelmerdine SC. *NEJM AI*, 2025. PMID: 42932526.]{.kw-ref}

This clinical evaluation case study describes how a five-hospital NHS trust in South West London used AI to flag suspected lung cancer on chest X-rays and route those patients to a radiographer-led same-day CT pathway. The authors compared 56,257 radiographs across one year before and two years after deployment, from January 2022 to December 2024. Time from chest X-ray to CT report for suspected cancer fell from 6.0 to 3.6 days, with the largest gains at sites where CT and X-ray sat together, and the proportion of CTs relative to X-rays did not rise significantly. For possible lung cancer, the 14-feature triage model ran at 82.5% sensitivity, 90.5% specificity, 14.6% positive predictive value and 99.6% negative predictive value. Focal airspace opacity and single nodules produced the most false positives, while masses gave the best yield. This is a before-and-after service evaluation rather than a controlled study, and the abstract does not report stage at diagnosis or survival. For cancer leads, it shows that the time saved depends as much on redesigning the CT pathway as on the algorithm, and that most flags will still not be cancer.

### 4. [External Validation of a Commercially Available AI Tool for Nasogastric Tube Position Decision Support in the NHS: A Prospective Silent Trial.](https://doi.org/10.1056/AIoa2500823)
[Bartsch AM, Packer J, Storey M, Togher D, Rickaby S, Dean G, Shelmerdine S. *NEJM AI*, 2026. PMID: 42932497.]{.kw-ref}

A misplaced nasogastric tube used for feeding is an NHS never event, so this NIHR-funded team ran a year-long prospective silent trial of a commercial, class 2b MDR-certified tool (Annalise Enterprise CXR) for judging tube position on chest X-ray. The AI's stand-alone output was compared with tube position across 1,605 consecutive radiographs taken for this purpose in one South West London NHS trust, without its results reaching clinicians. It correctly flagged 109 of 126 unsafely placed tubes, a sensitivity of 0.87 (95% CI 0.79–0.91), and correctly cleared 938 of 1,479 safe tubes, a specificity of 0.63 (95% CI 0.61–0.66). That meant 541 false alarms (34% of examinations) and a positive predictive value of 0.17, alongside 17 unsafe tubes it would have passed as safe. The negative predictive value was 0.98, but for a never event the authors conclude that this miss rate may make the tool unsuitable as the primary check. It is a single-trust study and the abstract does not detail how the reference standard was set. This is the kind of local silent evaluation every NHS trust should demand before switching on a certified feature: regulatory approval did not guarantee the safety performance this task needs.

### 5. [Examining reliance patterns on AI advice in medical imaging: a mixed-methods, randomised, crossover experiment.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.landig.2026.101050)
[Gaube S, Jussupow E, Kokje E, Koch TK, Khan J, Bondi-Kelly E, Schicho A, Kitamura FC, Ezer T, Mottok J, Lermer E, Ghassemi M, Colak E. *Lancet Digit Health*, 2026. PMID: 42919730.]{.kw-ref}

This preregistered experiment asked 50 radiologists and 75 non-radiologist doctors and trainees to read head CTs for intracranial haemorrhage in three sessions, randomising the order of no AI, a bare AI prediction, and an explainable AI prediction with annotations on the scan. Each participant read 50 scans per session, and a fifth of the AI advice was deliberately wrong, so the authors could measure both over-reliance (following wrong advice) and under-reliance (rejecting right advice). Both happened. Under-reliance, which tracked high uncertainty, did more damage to diagnostic accuracy in absolute terms than over-reliance. When the explainable advice was correct, it improved accuracy compared with no advice (OR 1.84, 95% CI 1.49–2.28) and raised confidence, particularly on harder positive cases, but did not shorten reading time. Novices found explainable advice more useful than the bare prediction. This was a reader experiment with a fixed error rate rather than clinical practice, so real-world reliance may differ. For NHS departments adopting triage or detection AI, it is a reminder that training should address clinicians discounting correct output, not only automation bias, and that heat maps alone do not fix either.

### 6. [Impact of Unrestricted Artificial Intelligence Scribe Deployment in a Single Health System on Clinician Workload and Productivity : A Quality Improvement Study.](https://doi.org/10.7326/ANNALS-25-05294)
[Booth SE, Gould R, Cibotti N, Fields R, Horng S, Jegadeesan V, Li S, Narayan D, Rubins DM, O'Donoghue AL, Simrak A, Stevens JP. *Ann Intern Med*, 2026. PMID: 42932880.]{.kw-ref}

A 14-hospital Boston health system made the Heidi ambient AI scribe available to outpatient clinicians from January 2025, and this retrospective quality improvement study used an interrupted time series indexed to each clinician's enrolment month. It covered 902 enrolled clinicians, 605 of whom used the tool and 297 who did not, and more than 1.6 million encounters between July 2024 and January 2026, adjusted for patient demographics and visit complexity. Enrolment was associated with an immediate drop in active note-writing time of 1.21 minutes per note (95% CI 0.68–1.74), with the largest fall among high users (2.50 minutes). High users also wrote longer notes, by roughly 170 characters more than non-users. There was no change in same-day note closure, after-hours closure or work relative value units. The design is observational, and after enrolment the authors could not tell AI-drafted notes from clinician-written ones. For NHS organisations procuring ambient scribes, the evidence so far supports a saving of a minute or two per note for committed users, not a step change in after-hours work or throughput.

### 7. [AI-Generated Draft Response Tool, Message Turnaround Time, and After-Hours Replies Among Health Care Professionals.](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.41364)
[Jeanselme V, Austin C, Han J, Lewis RA, Hruby GW, Natarajan K, Joshi S. *JAMA Netw Open*, 2026. PMID: 42961417.]{.kw-ref}

Columbia University Irving Medical Center deployed Epic's In Basket Augmented Response Technology, which drafts AI replies to patient portal messages, across the enterprise in December 2024. This retrospective cohort used clinician-level panel regression with individual fixed effects on 983,154 first responses from 1,542 clinicians to 272,091 patients between March 2023 and May 2025. The findings point in different directions. Adopting the tool was associated with an 8.6% longer overall turnaround time (95% CI 4.6%–12.9%), whereas the individual replies where the draft was actually used went out 29.5% faster (95% CI 24.1%–34.5%). Overall after-hours replying did not change. Using the tool was associated with fewer after-hours replies to test-result queries received in working hours (−3.67 percentage points) but more after-hours replies to messages that arrived out of hours (+4.52 points), and these after-hours results depended on how working hours were defined. The study is observational and from one US centre. As NHS App messaging grows, it suggests that drafted replies may make some messages easier to answer without reducing overall inbox burden, so trusts should measure workload directly rather than assume a saving.

### 8. [Overuse and False Restraint in Large Language Model Recommendations for Choosing Wisely Scenarios.](https://doi.org/10.7326/ANNALS-26-01667)
[Ariel D, Endelman S, Laban G. *Ann Intern Med*, 2026. PMID: 42896192.]{.kw-ref}

The authors turned 15 Choosing Wisely recommendations into 225 clinician-perspective scenarios, ten per recommendation where holding back was right and five where acting was right, and put them to six commercial large language models through the OpenAI, Anthropic and Google production APIs in February and March 2026. Running each model three times produced 4,050 responses, classified by an LLM judge with physician adjudication. Overall, the models recommended low-value action in 5.4% of responses (95% CI 0.6%–12.2%) and withheld appropriate action in only 0.6% (95% CI 0.1%–1.2%). Overuse was concentrated: models advised thyroid ultrasound for an incidental subcentimetre nodule in 42.8% of responses and routine ECGs in low-risk adults in 28.3%, while for eight recommendations they never advised overuse. False restraint was highest, at 3.3%, for PSA screening. This is a single-prompt benchmark without follow-up questions, not observed clinical use, and may not apply to patient-facing chatbots. For clinicians who use these models to sense-check investigations, the safety concern is less that they withhold care and more that they echo a few well-known low-value tests.
